sentences.text: Cartorhynchus was a small marine reptile measuring about 40 cm in length and weighing only 2 kilograms, possessing a lizard-like body with a short torso.
Its skull featured an unusually short snout that occupied half the skull's length, paired with a deep jaw.
The animal exhibited a striking contrast in bone development, having a well-ossified skull and vertebrae while its limbs remained poorly ossified.
Detailed examination revealed that the limbs contained only three hand digits that were ossified, with widely spaced bones suggesting extensive cartilage was present.
Fossils of this species show characteristics that likely allowed it to move on land.
At the time of its discovery, Cartorhynchus was the smallest known member of the Ichthyosauriformes.
The extensive cartilage at its wrist joint likely allowed its flippers to bend without an elbow, a feature similar to that seen in juvenile sea turtles.
The fossil was discovered in 2011 by Ryosuke Motani and Da-yong Jiang in a mine at Majiashan, Anhui, China.
The specimen was assigned the field number MT-II and the specimen number AGB 6257 at the Anhui Geological Museum.
The fossil is well-preserved except for part of the tail.
Ryosuke Motani and colleagues described the specimen as a new genus and species, Cartorhynchus lenticarpus, in Nature in 2014.
Because the specimen was too fragile to open, Jian-Dong Huang, Motani, and colleagues used micro-CT scanning performed at the Yinghua Testing Company in Shanghai to examine the interior of the jaws.
Cartorhynchus possessed molariform teeth, indicating a diet that included hard-shelled animals such as small ammonites, bivalves, and the thylacocephalan arthropod Ankitokazocaris.
Researchers suggest Cartorhynchus preyed on hard-shelled invertebrates using suction feeding, though the exact mechanism of its inward-directed teeth remains unknown.
Some researchers proposed that the animal likely fed by suction on soft-bodied creatures living on the sea floor.
Based on its body shape and large flippers, Cartorhynchus was likely not a fast swimmer.
Researchers suggested Cartorhynchus had an amphibious lifestyle aided by a short trunk, snout, and thickened ribs acting as ballast.
Researchers proposed that the unusual wear patterns on Cartorhynchus teeth might be due to jaw twisting during preservation or the loss of soft tissues, though neither fully explains the evidence.
Phylogenetic analyses indicate that Cartorhynchus is the most basal member of the clade Ichthyosauriformes.
Cartorhynchus belongs to the clade Nasorostra, which is the sister group to Ichthyopterygia.
In 2014, researchers named the group containing Cartorhynchus and Ichthyopterygia Ichthyosauriformes, and the larger group including Hupehsuchia Ichthyosauromorpha.
Cartorhynchus fits within the group Ichthyosauromorpha, which includes Ichthyosauriformes and Hupehsuchia as sister groups.
Cartorhynchus was part of a rapid diversification of marine reptiles during the Spathian substage, occurring about one million years after the Permian-Triassic extinction event.
Cartorhynchus lived during the Early Triassic epoch, approximately 248 million years ago.
More precise dating places the animal at approximately 248.41 million years ago.
It lived at the beginning of the Lower Triassic, specifically the Olenekian stage, approximately 248 million years ago.
Cartorhynchus lived in an oceanic basin located relatively far from the coast during the Middle Triassic.
Researchers suggest that the inability of the lower jaw bones to fuse tightly in Cartorhynchus was a characteristic shared with toothless hupehsuchians.
While researchers hypothesized in 2014 that Cartorhynchus was a suction feeder, a 2020 study concluded that it was a durophagous feeder based on its molariform teeth.
Researchers suggested Cartorhynchus was an adult exhibiting paedomorphosis, but acknowledged the possibility it was a juvenile given only one specimen exists.

Researchers believe the Cartorhynchus fossil may belong to a juvenile individual due to its small size, large eye orbits, short beak, and poorly ossified phalanges, though it is debated whether the specimen belonged to a juvenile individual.
